Housing Price Modeling in R: Multiple Regression, Interaction Effects, and Quadratic Regression¶

Project Overview¶

This project examines how property characteristics—including living area, number of bedrooms and bathrooms, home age, construction quality, neighborhood crime rate, school ratings, and property views—relate to residential sale prices. Multiple regression models were developed in R to estimate sale prices and evaluate the predictive importance of these characteristics. The analysis also explores interactions between qualitative variables and quadratic relationships that may not be adequately represented by a standard linear model.

Variables used in the analysis:

Variable
What does it represent?
price
Sale price of the home
bedrooms
Number of bedrooms
bathrooms
Number of bathrooms
sqft_living
Size of the living area in sqft
sqft_above
Size of the upper level in sqft
sqft_lot
Size of the lot in sqft
age
Age of the home
grade
Measure of craftsmanship and the quality of materials used to build the home
appliance_age
Average age of all appliances in the home
crime
Crime rate per 100,000 people
backyard
Home has a backyard (backyard=1) or not (backyard=0)
school_rating
Average rating of schools in the area
view
Home backs out to a lake (view=2), backs out to trees (view=1), or backs out to a road (view=0)

Preparing The Data Set¶

In [2]:
housing <- read.csv(file="housing_v2.csv", header=TRUE, sep=",")

# Convert appropriate variables to factors  
housing <- within(housing, {
   view <- factor(view)
   backyard <- factor(backyard)
})

# number of columns
ncol(housing)

# number of rows
nrow(housing)
23
2692

Model #1 - First Order Regression Model with Quantitative and Qualitative Variables¶

First order regression model with price as the response variable, and sqft_living, sqft_above, age, bathrooms, and view as predictor variables.

In [58]:
# Scatterplot of Price vs. Living Area
plot(housing$sqft_living, housing$price, 
     main = "Scatterplot of Price vs. Living Area",
     xlab = "Living Area", ylab = "Price",
     col="green", 
     pch = 19, frame = FALSE)
In [59]:
# Scatterplot of Price vs. Age
plot(housing$age, housing$price, 
     main = "Scatterplot of Price vs. Age",
     xlab = "Age", ylab = "Price",
     col="purple", 
     pch = 19, frame = FALSE)
In [43]:
myvars <- c("price","sqft_living", "age")
housing_subset <- housing[myvars]

# Print the correlation matrix
print("cor")
corr_matrix <- cor(housing_subset, method = "pearson")
round(corr_matrix, 4)

# Create the first order regression model and print the statistics
model1 <- lm(price ~ sqft_living + sqft_above + age + bathrooms + view, data=housing)
summary(model1)

In [4]:
# Predicted price for a home that has 2150 sqft living area, 1050 sqft upper level living area,
# is 15 years old, has 3 bathrooms, and backs out to road:
newdata <- data.frame(sqft_living=2150, sqft_above=1050, age=15, bathrooms=3, view='0')

print("prediction interval")
prediction_pred_int <- predict(model1, newdata, interval="predict", level=0.90) 
round(prediction_pred_int, 4)

print("confidence interval")
prediction_conf_int <- predict(model1, newdata, interval="confidence", level=0.90) 
round(prediction_conf_int, 4)

Model #2 - Complete Second Order Regression Model with Quantitative Variables¶

Complete second order regression model with price as the response variable, and school_rating and crime as predictor variables.

In [7]:
# Scatterplot of Price vs. Average School Rating
plot(housing$school_rating, housing$price, 
     main = "Scatterplot of Price vs. Average School Rating",
     xlab = "School rating", ylab = "Price",
     col="green", 
     pch = 19, frame = FALSE)
In [8]:
# Scatterplot of Price vs. Crime
plot(housing$crime, housing$price, 
     main = "Scatterplot of Price vs. Crime",
     xlab = "Crime", ylab = "Price",
     col="purple", 
     pch = 19, frame = FALSE)
In [10]:
# Create the second order regression model and print the statistics
model2 <- lm(price ~ school_rating + crime + school_rating:crime + I(school_rating^2) + I(crime^2), data=housing)
summary(model2)

Call:
lm(formula = price ~ school_rating + crime + school_rating:crime + 
    I(school_rating^2) + I(crime^2), data = housing)

Nested Models F-Test¶

Comparison of the reduced model (Model 3) and the complete second order model (Model #2 above).

In [56]:
# Create the first order regression model and print the statistics
model3 <- lm(price ~ school_rating + crime + school_rating:crime, data=housing)
summary(model3)
